posts.title: MOOWR in simple words: pay customs duty later, not at the port
posts.excerpt: A plain explanation of the scheme, with an example, for anyone who imports and manufactures in India.
posts.body:
Normally, when you bring goods into India, you pay customs duty at the port before you can take them out. For a factory that imports machines or raw materials, that is a large amount of cash paid long before any product is made or sold.

MOOWR is a scheme that lets you pay that duty later. The name stands for Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019. It works under section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962.

## The idea in one line

You keep your imported goods in a customs-approved warehouse (a bonded warehouse), do your manufacturing there, and pay duty only when the goods leave for sale in India.

## A simple example

A company imports a machine and some raw material. Without the scheme, it pays duty on both at the port, then waits months to earn money from the product. With the scheme, the goods go into the bonded warehouse without duty at that stage. The company makes its product. If it sells in India, duty is paid when the goods leave the warehouse. If it exports, no import duty is charged on the imported goods used.

## Who it helps

- Factories that import machinery or raw materials
- Businesses that export a large part of what they make
- Businesses that want to keep cash for running the business instead of locking it in duty

## What you need to do

- Apply to the customs authority for permission and a licence for the warehouse
- Give a bond, which is a written promise to follow the rules and pay any duty that falls due
- Keep clear records of what comes in, what is used, what is made, and what goes out
- Send the returns and records that customs asks for, on time

## Things to think about first

- Duty is put off, not removed. Goods sold in India will still attract duty.
- The records are the heart of the scheme. Poor records can cause trouble later.
- The rules and how customs applies them change from time to time, so check the current position before you apply.
- It does not suit every business. It depends on what you import, what you make, and how much you sell in India and abroad.

## Is it right for you?

Whether MOOWR suits a business depends on what it imports, what it makes, and how much it sells in India and abroad. The official text is available in the Reading material section of this website.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EMI scheme in simple words: pay customs duty once a month
posts.excerpt: How the Eligible Manufacturer Importer facility lets approved manufacturers pay import duty monthly instead of at every clearance.
posts.body:
Normally, an importer pays customs duty on each consignment before the goods leave the port. For a factory that imports every week, that means paying duty again and again, often long before the finished product is sold.

The Eligible Manufacturer Importer (EMI) facility changes this for approved manufacturers. They can clear goods without paying duty at that moment, and pay the duty for all clearances together once a month.

## The basics

- It was introduced by CBIC Circular No. 08/2026-Customs, dated 28 February 2026.
- It works under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016.
- It is available from 1 April 2026 and stays in force until 31 March 2028.

## A simple example

A manufacturer imports components on several dates in a month. Without the facility, it pays duty on every Bill of Entry at the time of clearance. As an approved EMI, it clears all the shipments first, and pays the total duty by the 1st of the next month. For goods cleared in March, the payment is due by 31 March.

## Who can apply

The circular sets conditions on compliance, turnover, financial standing and track record. As reported, the main ones include:

- A valid Importer-Exporter Code and registration as a manufacturer under GST.
- A minimum number of import or export documents in the previous year (fewer for MSMEs).
- Turnover above a stated limit, and at least two years in business.
- GST returns filed, no unpaid tax collected, and a clean record under customs and tax laws.
- A Chartered Accountant's certificate showing financial soundness.

Existing AEO Tier 1 entities that meet these conditions can also apply. The circular itself has the full list and the exact figures.

## How it works

1. The application is made online on the AEO portal, under the Eligible Manufacturer Importer tab.
2. The Directorate of International Customs reviews it.
3. After approval, the status is updated in the customs system.
4. A nominated person gets an ICEGATE login to authenticate transactions.
5. On each Bill of Entry, the importer selects the deferred payment option and authenticates it with an OTP.

## Things to keep in mind

- The duty is deferred, not waived. It must be paid by the due date every month.
- The conditions must be met throughout the period. If they are not, or if payment is missed, the approval can be suspended or withdrawn.
- Circulars and portal procedures can change, so the current text should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EPCG scheme in simple words: import machinery without customs duty
posts.excerpt: What the Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme is, how the export obligation works, and what happens at the end.
posts.body:
A factory that wants to start exporting often needs new machinery, and importing it means paying customs duty. The Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) scheme helps with that cost. It is run by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade Policy.

## The idea in one line

You import capital goods at zero customs duty, and in return you promise to export a set value of goods within a set time.

## How the promise works

The promise is called the export obligation. Under Foreign Trade Policy 2023, it is generally:

- 6 times the duty saved,
- to be fulfilled within 6 years from the date of the authorisation.

A lower multiple applies in some cases, for example when the capital goods are bought from an Indian manufacturer. A separate average export obligation can also apply, so the authorisation itself should always be read closely.

## A simple example

Suppose the customs duty on a machine would normally be Rs 10 lakh. Under EPCG, the duty is not paid, so the duty saved is Rs 10 lakh. The exporter must then export goods worth 6 times that, which is Rs 60 lakh, within 6 years.

## Who can apply

- Manufacturer exporters
- Merchant exporters tied to a supporting manufacturer
- Service providers who earn foreign exchange

All of them need a valid Importer-Exporter Code (IEC).

## How to apply

- The application is filed online on the DGFT portal, before the import.
- It needs supporting papers, such as a Chartered Engineer's certificate for the machinery.
- When the goods are imported, customs takes a bond or other security for the duty saved.

## What happens at the end

The exporter submits proof of exports and realised foreign exchange. DGFT then issues the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate (EODC), which closes the authorisation.

If the obligation is not fulfilled, the duty saved on the unfulfilled part has to be paid back with interest. Extensions are possible in some cases, but the liability remains.

## Keep in mind

DGFT issues public notices from time to time that change deadlines, procedures and facilities for EPCG. The current notices and the Handbook of Procedures should be checked before acting.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EPR in simple words: what importers should know about Extended Producer Responsibility
posts.excerpt: What EPR means, which products it covers, and why it now matters at the customs counter.
posts.body:
When a product reaches the end of its life, someone has to collect and recycle it. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) puts that duty on the businesses that put the product on the market: the producers, brand owners and importers.

## What EPR means

A business covered by EPR has to register with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) through its online portal. It must then make sure a set share of its products is collected and recycled, usually through registered recyclers, and report this every year.

## Which products are covered

Each type of product has its own rules:

- Plastic packaging: the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended.
- Electrical and electronic equipment: the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.
- Batteries: the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022.
- Other rules cover items such as waste tyres and used oil.

## Why it matters to importers

An importer counts as a producer. If a business imports goods that fall under these rules and sells them in India, it has to register, even if it does not make anything in India.

Customs also looks at this now:

- For plastic, a CPCB direction dated 13 June 2025 asks importers of plastic packaging and of plastic raw material meant for packaging to register on the EPR portal. Customs has been asked to check for the registration before clearing such consignments.
- For electronic goods, customs can ask for proof of EPR registration, or a declaration, before clearance.

## What registration involves

- An account on the CPCB portal, using the business's IEC, PAN and GST details.
- Documents about the products imported and sold.
- For electronics, agreements with authorised recyclers and an EPR plan.
- Yearly returns showing that targets were met.

## Practical points

- Check whether the product's customs tariff heading falls under any of these rules.
- Register before the goods arrive, because clearance can be held up without it.
- Keep records of quantities imported and sold, since annual returns depend on them.

The rules and portal requirements are updated often, so the current CPCB notifications should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

library.title: The Customs Act, 1962
library.desc: The principal law on levy and collection of customs duty, import and export procedure, warehousing, baggage, penalties and appeals.

library.title: The Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 (FTDR Act)
library.desc: The law under which DGFT regulates imports and exports, issues the Foreign Trade Policy and grants authorisations such as the IEC.

library.title: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA)
library.desc: The law governing foreign exchange, cross-border payments, and foreign investment into and out of India.

library.title: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Rules, 2026 (FCRA)
library.desc: Gazette notification amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011.

library.title: Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse (No. 2) Regulations, 2019 (MOOWR)
library.desc: Notification 69/2019-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 October 2019. The rules for manufacturing and other operations in a bonded warehouse under section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962.

library.title: Warehoused Goods (Removal) Regulations, 2016
library.desc: Notification 67/2016-Customs (N.T.) dated 14 May 2016. How goods are removed from one warehouse to another, or for export, under the Customs Act, 1962.

library.title: The Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963
library.desc: Act No. 54 of 1963. Sets up the separate Central Boards for Direct Taxes and for Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), and how the Boards work.

library.title: The Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 (SEZ Act), as enacted
library.desc: Act No. 28 of 2005, in the form published in the Gazette of India on 23 June 2005, before later amendments.

library.title: The Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 (SEZ Act), amended up to February 2020
library.desc: Act No. 28 of 2005 with amendments up to February 2020, as compiled by the Export Promotion Council for EOUs and SEZs (EPCES). Includes the Schedules.

library.title: The Companies Act, 2013 (amended up to 2015)
library.desc: Act No. 18 of 2013, with amendments only up to the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015. Later amendments are not included, so check the latest version before relying on it.

library.title: Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 (original text)
library.desc: The rules for incorporating a company under the Companies Act, 2013, with the incorporation forms. This is the original 2014 text, without later amendments.

library.title: The Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 (LLP Act)
library.desc: Act No. 6 of 2009, as on 1 September 2026. The law on forming and running a limited liability partnership.

library.title: Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009 (original text)
library.desc: Notification G.S.R. 229(E) dated 1 April 2009, with the LLP forms. This is the original text, without later amendments.

library.title: The Patents Act, 1970
library.desc: Act No. 39 of 1970, with all amendments up to 1 August 2024. What can be patented, how to apply, and the rights of a patent holder.

library.title: The Trade Marks Act, 1999
library.desc: Act No. 47 of 1999. Registration, protection and infringement of trademarks, as amended.

library.title: The Copyright Act, 1957
library.desc: Act No. 14 of 1957, as amended, including the 2012 amendment. Copyright in literary, artistic, musical and software works.

library.title: The Designs Act, 2000
library.desc: Act No. 16 of 2000, as published in the Gazette. Registration and protection of the shape, pattern or ornament of a product.

library.title: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 (GI Act)
library.desc: Act No. 48 of 1999, last updated 27 July 2022. Protection of goods linked to a place, such as crafts, foods and farm produce.

library.title: The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000
library.desc: Act No. 37 of 2000. Registration and protection of layout-designs of semiconductor integrated circuits.

library.title: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 (PPV&FR Act)
library.desc: Act No. 53 of 2001, as published in the Gazette. Protection of new plant varieties and the rights of farmers and breeders.
